sources.title: Deutsches Historisches Museum, Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation 962 to 1806
sources.note: General Introduction and sections IV to VI: 962 to 1806, multilingual and decentralized polity, elections, 1495 reform, permanent Diet from 1663, Jewish legal status, Francis II abdication.

sources.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Ottonian Art
sources.note: Ottonian rulers and the metalwork, manuscript and church production of monastic workshops, including Bernward of Hildesheim.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Speyer Cathedral
sources.note: Brief synthesis: Conrad II foundation in 1030, Henry IV vaulting campaign, Romanesque architecture and imperial burials. Later repairs and rebuilding also noted.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, ShUM Sites of Speyer, Worms and Mainz
sources.note: Brief synthesis and criteria: 11th to 14th century Ashkenazic communal institutions, women’s shul, yeshiva remains, mikveh, cemeteries and continuing tradition. Worms synagogue has post-war reconstruction.

sources.title: Institut für Stadtgeschichte Frankfurt, Die Goldene Bulle
sources.note: Introduction and document: Charles IV’s 1356 Latin election law, archive-held 1366 Frankfurt copy, 1371 German translation and seven surviving official copies.

sources.title: Gerhard Köbler, text of the Golden Bull of Charles IV (1356)
sources.note: Transcription from Karl Zeumer’s edition, Nuremberg text, chapter preamble, original Latin words Omne regnum in se ipsum divisum desolabitur.

sources.title: Yale Law School Avalon Project, English translation of the Golden Bull of 1356
sources.note: Preamble translates the Latin phrase about a kingdom divided against itself and the law’s election provisions.

sources.title: Germanisches Nationalmuseum, Digital Story: Love, Marriage and Family
sources.note: Spielzeugstadt Nürnberg / Kruseler Made in Nürnberg section: mould-made Kruseler dolls, fashionable headdress, production and finds beginning in 14th century.

sources.title: Germanisches Nationalmuseum, Stromer Dollhouse
sources.note: Collection object HG4063, Nuremberg, 1639: 15 rooms and over 1,000 items, an idealized elite household model used for teaching household and business management, not ordinary doll play.

sources.title: Museums of Nuremberg, Dürer’s House over the Centuries
sources.note: 1509 to 1528 house included Dürer, wife Agnes, mother, pupils and apprentices; Nuremberg was a self-governing imperial city.

sources.title: Museums of Nuremberg, Historic Rooms of Fembo House
sources.note: Family hall about 1600, ceremonial versus living rooms; seventeenth/eighteenth century reconstructed rich merchant kitchen and documented food preservation.

sources.title: Nuremberg city tourism, Köttelgang
sources.note: Local tourism interpretation: surviving medieval shared latrine opening between houses on Obere Schmiedgasse; does not prove a uniform imperial sanitation system.

sources.title: Nuremberg tourism, Hospital of the Holy Spirit
sources.note: Hospital established by Konrad Gross in 1332 to 1339 to care for older and needy people; later regalia storage distinguished.

sources.title: UNESCO Memory of the World, 42-line Gutenberg Bible
sources.note: Gutenberg printing office in Mainz and contemporary Model Book and Helmasperger notarial record; printing spread from Mainz across Europe.

sources.title: Deutsches Historisches Museum, Reformation and the Thirty Years’ War
sources.note: Museum overview: printing helped spread Luther’s teaching, Augsburg settlement 1555, war 1618 to 1648, Westphalia settlement 1648; period objects include a ca. 1600 game board.

sources.title: The Met Cloisters, St John’s wort
sources.note: Hortus Sanitatis, a printed late medieval herbal, recommended St John’s wort for wounds and other uses; describes historical belief, not proven efficacy.

sources.title: Wellcome Collection, Hortus sanitatis catalogue
sources.note: Bibliographic record dates Jakob Meydenbach’s Mainz printing to 1491 and identifies the book as Latin.

sources.title: Germanisches Nationalmuseum, Digital Story: Life and Death
sources.note: Medicine discussion: faith and humoral medicine in late medieval life; historical explanations of bodily fluids, not current medicine.

scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

The museum’s 962 to 1806 convention refers to the imperial institution, not ancient Roman continuity or a modern German state. Dynastic and ecclesiastical power, electors, free cities, and shifting frontiers complicate a single polygon. The imported 1000 to 1783 span is not a historical lifetime; dateBasis historical records 962 to 1806 while leaving geometry unchanged.

ShUM sites document Jewish institutions and continuing Ashkenazic tradition within the medieval empire. Surviving Worms synagogue fabric includes modern reconstruction; no claim all medieval buildings are original. Jewish legal dependence and vulnerability are acknowledged, without reducing these communities to an imperial footnote.

The Latin sample quotes nine words from the 1356 Golden Bull in a scholarly transcription. The Frankfurt archive preserves an official 1366 copy and a later 1371 German translation; the card does not present its copy as Charles IV’s autograph or imply universal literacy. The quotation is Latin written in the Latin alphabet.

Kruseler figures are local Nuremberg mould-made toys, not an empire-wide or universal child experience. Dürer’s house, Fembo House and the Stromer miniature are elite urban cases from distinct dates. The dollhouse is an ideal teaching model, not a real home or a typical toy. The kitchen is museum reconstruction using period parts.

The Köttelgang is a local surviving medieval shared toilet. It is not evidence for flush toilets or sanitation prevalence throughout the empire. The hospital foundation documents a care institution and intended beneficiaries, not medical results. The herbal records historical recommendations, not effective or safe treatment.

The 1618 to 1648 war had political and religious dimensions and foreign involvement. The 1806 dissolution is institutional; there is no single replacement polity or population extinction. No successor link has been added without checking event-year target geometry and identity.
All narrative author-checked and awaiting independent review. Imported border polygons remain unverified. This unassigned Europe record was claimed without altering QWEN-owned Asia entries.

proposedOverrides.summary: For centuries, the Holy Roman Empire linked many central European rulers, towns and communities under an elected emperor. Its borders and powers changed, while workshops, schools, printing presses and households shaped life beyond the court. Francis II gave up the imperial crown in 1806; the people and their cultures continued.
